result.summary: Ulysses and Telemachus hide the armour, and Ulysses is left to talk with Penelope. In disguise he tells her a false Cretan tale and swears Ulysses is near; Euryclea recognises his scar while washing his feet and is sworn to silence. Penelope tells her dream of the eagle and geese and announces the contest of the axes.

scenes.title: Removing the armour
scenes.summary: Ulysses has Telemachus store the weapons away. Minerva lights their way, and Telemachus sees the glow and goes to bed.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses must prepare to kill the suitors without revealing himself too soon.

scenes.title: Melantho rebuked; Penelope questions
scenes.summary: Melantho abuses Ulysses and is scolded by Penelope. Penelope asks the stranger who he is, and he deflects.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses risks exposure and further abuse as a beggar.

scenes.title: Penelope's web
scenes.summary: Penelope tells of the suitors and of the shroud she wove and unpicked for three years.
scenes.stakes: She may be forced to marry one of the suitors.

scenes.title: Ulysses' Cretan tale
scenes.summary: Ulysses claims to be Aethon, brother of Idomeneus, who hosted Ulysses in Crete, and describes his clothes.
scenes.stakes: He must convince Penelope without revealing himself.

scenes.title: Oath and offer of a bath
scenes.summary: Penelope weeps at the proofs. Ulysses swears her husband is alive and returning, and asks that only an old woman wash his feet.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses hopes Penelope will believe him while he stays hidden.

scenes.title: The scar's story
scenes.summary: As Euryclea washes him, the narrator tells how Ulysses was named and wounded by a boar on Parnassus.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses was wounded hunting the boar.

scenes.title: Euryclea recognises him
scenes.summary: Euryclea drops his foot, and Ulysses threatens her into silence. She promises, and finishes the bath.
scenes.stakes: If Euryclea tells, Ulysses' plan against the suitors is ruined.

scenes.title: Penelope's dream and the axes
scenes.summary: Penelope tells of her eagle dream, Ulysses reads it as the suitors' doom, and she announces the contest of the bow and axes before retiring.
scenes.stakes: Penelope may be forced to leave Ulysses' house with a suitor.

alias_notes.explanation: The false name Ulysses gives himself in his Cretan tale.

notable_quotes.reason: Penelope's gates of horn and ivory for true and false dreams.
Penelope's line that he cannot be the son of an oak or rock.

analysis.text: Recognition and disguise: Ulysses is nearly known by Euryclea's touch while Penelope half-tests him, and truth is mixed with lies.
Guest-friendship and hospitality govern the scene, as when Penelope honours the stranger and Ulysses insists on a respectable old servant.

legacy.text: The gates of horn and ivory became a lasting image for true and false dreams, reused by Virgil in the Aeneid.
Auerbach's Mimesis (1946) opens with the scar scene to contrast Homeric and biblical narrative.

fun_facts.text: The scar episode is a famous digression, interrupting the washing to narrate Ulysses' naming and boar hunt.

language_notes.text: The cloister is the covered colonnade or hall of the house, here the great hall where the suitors feast.
Begrimed means covered with ingrained dirt; the armour is blackened by years of hearth smoke.
"Set them on to quarrel" means Jove might provoke them to fight; the excuse blames divine influence for drunken brawling.
Smirched means smeared or stained.
Radiance means shining light; the lamp's glow is supernatural and fills the whole hall.
"The manner of the gods" means this is how gods behave: they appear unseen and should not be questioned.
Venus and Diana are the goddesses of love and of the chaste hunt; the comparison praises Penelope's beauty and her purity.
Braziers are metal containers that hold burning charcoal or wood for heating and light; the hall has no chimney lamps.
"Rail" means to scold or abuse loudly and bitterly.
"Wanton" here means to behave insolently and carelessly, taking liberties because of one's secure position.
"By Apollo's will" means that the god permitted Telemachus to be born and survive. Ulysses is hinting at his own return and at the son's coming vengeance.
"Baggage" is an old term of abuse for a worthless or shameless woman.
"Chide with you" means to quarrel or find fault with you.
"Firmament of heaven" is the vault of the sky, imagined as a solid dome.
"Argives" is Homer's common name for the Greeks, taken from Argos; here it means the whole Greek army at Troy.
A "tambour-frame" is an embroidery hoop; the word is a Victorian rendering for the loom on which Penelope weaves her web.
"Pall" means a funeral cloth or shroud laid over or wrapped around a corpse.
"Sweethearts" is ironic address; she is speaking to the suitors with false sweetness.
"In the waning of moons" means as months passed and the year was running out; "hussies" is the translator's word for disloyal maids.
"Son of an oak or of a rock" is a proverbial phrase: only people of unknown origin were thought to spring from trees or stones.
Eteocretans ("true Cretans"), Dorians and Pelasgi were peoples associated with Crete; the list reflects its mixed population, here told by Ulysses to sound convincing.
Minos's nine-year conference with Jove refers to a tradition that he received laws from Jove (the Greek Zeus) in periodic meetings.
"Subscriptions" means contributions collected from the townspeople to supply wine and oxen for the visitors.
"Elsewhither" is an archaic word meaning "to some other place."
"Fitted him like the skin of an onion" means the shirt was thin, fine and smooth, like onion skin.
The detested city is Troy; Penelope blames the Trojan War for taking Ulysses away, and cannot bear to name it.
Thrinacian island is where Ulysses' men slaughtered the sun-god's cattle, an earlier event in his wanderings; Jove then destroyed the ship.
Dodona was a famous oracle of Jove, where the god's will was read from the rustling of a sacred oak.
Swearing by the hearth of Ulysses invokes the household's sacred centre, a binding oath for a guest.
Cloister means the covered colonnade or hall of the house, where the household gathered.
Hussies here means pert, ill-mannered young servant girls.
Age-mate means someone of the same age; Penelope says Ulysses would now look as aged as the beggar.
Hecatombs were large public sacrifices, originally of a hundred oxen; here simply splendid offerings to the god.
"Gibing" means jeering or mocking; "sluts" is the translator's blunt word for the disloyal maidservants.
"Perjurer" means one who swears false oaths; Autolycus's skill at deceit is presented as a talent.
The name Ulysses is explained through a Greek word play on anger or hatred; Autolycus names the boy for the resentment he feels toward others.
"Child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn" is a stock Homeric phrase for daybreak.
Saying a spell to stop bleeding refers to an old practice of healing wounds with chanted charms.
The scar on Ulysses' leg came from a boar's tusk in his youth; Euryclea knows it from having washed him as a child.
"Diverted her attention" means Minerva (Athena) kept Penelope from noticing, so the recognition stays secret.
The nightingale myth: Pandareus' daughter killed her son Itylus by mistake and was turned into a nightingale, who mourns him in song.
"Her seat in shadiest covert hid" is a poetic, inverted way of saying she sings hidden in thick foliage.
Dreams were thought to pass through two gates: ivory for deceptive dreams, horn for true ones. This is a famous Homeric image.
"Fatuous" here means empty or deceptive, carrying no real meaning.
The "city with a hateful name" is Troy (Ilium), which Penelope hates for taking her husband away.

context_notes.text: Minerva (the Greek Athene) is Ulysses' protector goddess, who guides his plan to take revenge on the suitors who have overrun his house.
Euryclea is Ulysses' old nurse, who once nursed Telemachus too and now supervises the household women.
Telemachus is speaking of Ulysses, who is disguised as a beggar; no one but father and son knows who he really is.
Telemachus' room opens on the inner court, away from the great hall where Ulysses remains.
Icmalius is a craftsman named only here. A footstool made in one piece with the chair marks it as fine work.
Eurynome is the housekeeper, the chief woman servant of the household, and she is trusted by Penelope.
Asking a stranger his name, city and parents was a normal courtesy in Homeric hospitality, usually after he had been fed.
Dulichium, Same and Zacynthus are islands near Ithaca; nobles from all of them court Penelope, hoping to become king by marrying her.
Laertes is Ulysses' aged father. Providing a proper burial shroud was a serious duty, which made her excuse believable.
The maids who betrayed her were serving the suitors; this foreshadows their later punishment by Ulysses.
Idomeneus was the king of Crete who led its fleet to Troy. Ulysses invents a brother relationship with him to seem credible.
The detailed brooch and cloak are a test of Ulysses' claim: Penelope asks for details only her real guest could know.
Eurybates was Ulysses' herald and trusted attendant in the Odyssey.
The Thesprotians were a people of Epirus, in northwestern Greece. Ulysses invents or reports a story of his stay with them.
The Phaeacians were a seafaring people who, in the story, hosted Ulysses and sent him home.
Euryclea is the old nurse who raised Ulysses. Her washing of the stranger's feet leads to the famous scar scene.
The scar will let Euryclea recognise Ulysses, the nurse who raised him, after twenty years away.
Mercury (the Greek Hermes) was patron of thieves and trickery, so Autolycus's gifts for theft come from him.
Oceanus was imagined as a great river encircling the world, from which the sun rose each day.
Ulysses threatens to kill even his old nurse because revealing him would ruin his plan to surprise and slaughter the suitors.
Washing a guest's feet was a standard act of hospitality, usually done by an old female servant.
The test requires shooting an arrow cleanly through the holes of twelve axe heads set in a line, a feat only Ulysses has managed.

literary_notes.text: Ulysses tells his son to say the armour has suffered since Ulysses left, though he himself is the absent master, now present and planning to use it.
The golden lamp and the walls glowing as with flaming fire give a vivid picture of divine presence in the dark hall.
The closing line repeats the scene's opening almost word for word, framing the episode and showing Ulysses' unbroken focus on vengeance.
Ulysses' invented past as a rich man who gave to beggars makes his disguise convincing, and it hints at his true former wealth and generosity.
Ulysses warns Melantho that Ulysses may return, and the audience knows he is already there, speaking to her.
Ulysses compares Penelope's fame to a just king whose virtue brings fertile land, flocks and fish. This flatters her and also deflects her question.
He claims that people might think him drunk, while the real reason for his tears is his long grief and the emotion of seeing his wife.
Penelope presents herself as resourceful and cunning, like her husband; she survives by "stratagems" rather than force.
Weaving by day and unpicking by night shows Penelope's cleverness and her faithfulness through endless delay.
Penelope presses the stranger about his family without knowing she is speaking to her own husband in disguise.
Calling his stories "plausible" marks Ulysses as a skilled, cunning liar, a trait central to his character.
Penelope's tears are compared to melting mountain snow feeding swollen rivers, conveying how her grief floods out once softened.
The audience knows Ulysses is the husband she weeps for, so his hardened eyes show painful, deliberate self-control.
The brooch's image of a dog gripping a struggling fawn may echo Ulysses' own predatory cunning, and the helpless suitors, though the poem does not say so.
Ulysses, speaking of himself in the third person, praises his own cunning, matching his epithet as the wily hero.
Penelope doubts the return of the very man who sits before her, though the reader knows the stranger is Ulysses.
Mentioning the nurse who received Ulysses at birth hints that she may recognise him when she washes his feet.
Euryclea notes that the most pious man is hated by Jove, unaware that the beggar before her is Ulysses himself.
Ulysses accepts her remark about the resemblance with calm cunning, while the audience knows why they look alike.
His turning from the light signals that the scar will expose him and sets up the recognition.
The dense, dark thicket, shut off from wind, rain and sun, builds menace before the boar appears.
The boar with bristling neck and fiery eyes is rendered as a fierce, almost heroic opponent.
The overturned bath and Euryclea's cry nearly expose Ulysses, while the audience knows what Penelope does not.
Comparing her silence to stone or iron stresses Euryclea's firmness and loyalty.
The long nightingale comparison shows Penelope's restless, grieving mind through an extended mythic image.
The eagle stands for Ulysses and the geese for the suitors, making the dream an allegory of the coming slaughter.
Ulysses, speaking as a stranger, promises his own return to his wife, who does not realize who he is.
